messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The toxic exposure happened eighteen months ago, but for Mai, the memory had never settled into the past. She had been prepping her workstation at the tattoo studio, mixing a new batch of pigment from a supplier she had used for years, when a chemical reaction she had not anticipated sent a plume of acrid fumes straight into her face. Within seconds her throat had seized, her lungs had burned, and she could not draw a full breath. A fellow artist called 911, and Mai remembered the ride to the emergency room as a blur of sirens and the terrifying sensation of not being in control of her own body. At the hospital, things only got worse. She was placed on supplemental oxygen, and the staff came in and out of her room constantly—checking her vitals, adjusting the nasal cannula, asking the same questions over and over. She recalled feeling propped up on the bed like a specimen, unable to move without permission, her arms prickling from the IV line they had inserted despite her saying she did not want one. The room smelled sharply of antiseptic and hand sanitizer, a smell that seemed to coat the inside of her nose and stay there for days after she was discharged.

Back at home, the physical symptoms faded, but something else had taken root. Mai found herself hyperaware of scents she had never registered before. The hand sanitizer pump at the grocery store entrance made her stomach drop. A whiff of rubbing alcohol from a first-aid kit sent a flash of heat through her chest. She started buying unscented soap and asking her husband to stop using the spray disinfectant he liked in the bathroom. When her mother called to say she had been hospitalized briefly for a minor procedure, Mai could not bring herself to visit. The idea of walking into a room that smelled like that again made her feel like she could not get enough air.

The studio had always been her sanctuary, but now it contained its own version of the same smell. The alcohol wipes, the sterilizing solution, the barrier film—she could not escape them. She learned to tolerate them by holding her breath and looking away, but the work itself began to feel different. Mai had always prided herself on collaborating with clients, listening to their ideas, incorporating their vision. Now, when a client leaned over the chair to watch her needle work, she felt a tightness in her jaw that had nothing to do with concentration. She had come to interpret being watched as a kind of surveillance, as though they were waiting for her to make a mistake, or worse, trying to catch her doing something wrong. She began positioning her body to block their view, angling the chair away, asking them to sit back and relax—phrases that used to come easily but now felt like small negotiations for space.

The same discomfort surfaced whenever a client pushed back on a design choice or asked for a change mid-session. Mai had always been flexible, happy to adjust. But now, being told what to do—even politely—stirred something hot and resistant in her chest. She had started to refuse certain requests outright, citing hygiene or safety reasons, though she knew deep down that her refusal was about something else. She could not stand the feeling of being forced, even when the force was just a customer's preference. Several regulars had stopped booking with her, and her income had dropped by nearly a third over the past six months. Her husband had asked her what was going on, and she had told him she was fine, because she did not know how to explain it. What was there to say? That a chemical spill had rearranged her entire sense of safety inside her own shop? That she could not tell the difference anymore between a client watching her work and a doctor watching her breathe?

What finally brought Mai to seek help was a single moment. A new client came in for a consultation, sat down in the chair, and the first thing she did was pull out a small bottle of hand sanitizer from her purse and offer it to Mai. The gesture was kind, meant to be friendly. Mai looked at the bottle, caught the faint antiseptic scent, and felt her throat close. She excused herself to the bathroom, locked the door, and stood there with her hands on the sink, trembling. She was not sure anymore how much more of this she could manage on her own. She was afraid that if she did not find a way through it, she would lose her business, her steady sense of herself, and the one thing that had always felt like her own: her art.
